prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Late winter, almost spring. It's like finding a diamond; now I don't want to leave. I sit in the dirt and put my hands in your tracks. For the first time in a long time I don't doubt. Now I know I always knew you were here. You are the beginning of disclosure, the long-felt presence Suddenly incarnate. Behind me my friend warns, If we see the bear, get into a fetal position. No problem, I tell her, I'm always in a fetal position—I was born in a fetal position. Did you know, she says, the body of a shaved bear looks exactly like a human man? I skip a stone, feel a sudden bloat of grief, then laugh. I ask her, Who would shave a bear? We climb Farther up Rattlesnake Creek, watch winter sun glitter off dark water. No matter how high we go I look higher. Sometimes absence can prove presence. That's not exactly faith, I know. All day, everywhere, I feel you near at hand. There's so much to understand, and everything to prove. Up high the air is thin and hard, roars in the ears like love.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Late, For, Now

outputs.L1:
Late winter, almost spring. It is like finding a diamond; now I do not want to leave. I sit in the dirt and place my hands in your tracks. For the first time in a long time, I do not doubt. Now I know that I always knew you were here. You are the beginning of disclosure, the long-felt presence suddenly incarnate.

Behind me, my friend warns, “If we see the bear, get into a fetal position.”

“No problem,” I tell her. “I’m always in a fetal position—I was born in a fetal position.”

“Did you know,” she says, “that the body of a shaved bear looks exactly like a human man?”

I skip a stone, feel a sudden swell of grief, then laugh. “Who would shave a bear?” I ask.

We climb farther up Rattlesnake Creek and watch the winter sun glitter on the dark water. No matter how high we go, I look higher. Sometimes absence can prove presence. That is not exactly faith, I know.

All day, everywhere, I feel you near at hand. There is so much to understand, and everything to prove. Up high, the air is thin and hard; it roars in the ears like love.
outputs.L2:
Winter is nearly over, and spring is close. The discovery feels as rare as a diamond, and I no longer want to go. I lower myself onto the earth and press my palms into the marks you left behind. For the first time in ages, uncertainty disappears. I understand now that some part of me has always known you were here. You are the first sign of revelation, a presence sensed for years abruptly given flesh.

Behind me, my friend says that if the bear appears, we should curl into fetal positions. Easy enough, I reply—I’m always curled that way; it’s how I entered the world. She asks whether I know that, without its fur, a bear’s body looks exactly like a man’s.

I send a flat rock skimming across the water, am suddenly swollen with sorrow, and then begin to laugh. Who, I ask, would ever shave a bear?

We continue higher along Rattlesnake Creek, watching the low winter sunlight flash across the black water. However far we climb, my eyes keep searching above us. At times, what is missing can serve as evidence that something exists. I realize that isn’t quite the same as faith.

Throughout the day, wherever I am, I sense you close by. There is an immense amount left to comprehend, and all of it still needs proof. At this elevation, the air is sharp and scarce, thundering inside the ears the way love does.
outputs.L3:
In late winter, the speaker discovers bear tracks in the snow and immediately feels certain that the animal is nearby, even though it remains unseen. The tracks transform an intuition into something tangible: what the speaker has long sensed now seems real, physical, and embodied. This moment carries the force of a revelation, as if the bear’s invisible presence has suddenly entered the visible world through the marks it has left behind.

As the speaker hikes with a friend, the two joke about what they might do if they actually encounter the bear. Their humor does not erase the danger; instead, it brings fear, grief, and laughter together, revealing the emotional complexity of the experience. Continuing upward along Rattlesnake Creek, the speaker begins to reflect on the paradox of presence and absence. The bear cannot be seen, yet its absence does not make it unreal. On the contrary, the tracks suggest that what is missing from sight may still be powerfully present.

The surrounding landscape deepens this realization. The elevation, the sharp winter air, and the rushing sound of the creek heighten the speaker’s awareness of the natural world and of their own emotions. In this cold, vast setting, wonder becomes intertwined with longing and love. The unseen bear, like anything deeply desired or mourned, is felt most strongly through the signs it leaves behind.
outputs.L4:
Following bear tracks up Rattlesnake Creek, the speaker turns a simple walk into a meditation on loss, belief, and the mysteries of the natural world. The tracks invite close attention: each print, disturbance, and change in the landscape becomes evidence of an animal that remains just out of sight. The speaker’s careful observations are balanced by moments of humor, preventing the search from becoming overly solemn and showing how wonder can coexist with pain.

As the speaker continues, the unseen bear begins to represent more than a physical animal. Its absence recalls other forms of absence, including grief and the longing for what has been lost or cannot be fully known. Yet the bear is not entirely absent. Its tracks prove that it has passed through the creek, leaving behind signs that can be read and followed. In this way, the landscape becomes a place where uncertainty and faith meet: the speaker cannot see the bear, but its presence is made convincing through the marks it leaves.

The journey gradually transforms doubt into conviction. Rather than treating absence as emptiness, the speaker comes to understand it as another way presence may be revealed. What cannot be directly seen may still be felt, remembered, or recognized through its effects. The bear’s tracks therefore become a source of reassurance, suggesting that love, memory, and spiritual presence can endure even when their objects remain beyond reach.

By the end, the search has renewed the speaker’s capacity for wonder. Close attention to the tracks opens a deeper awareness of connection—between human beings and animals, grief and faith, the visible world and what lies beyond it. The unseen bear becomes a long-felt presence, reminding the speaker that mystery need not be overcome in order to inspire belief. Through following what remains, the speaker rediscovers love and learns that absence itself can sometimes be the clearest sign that something meaningful is still present.
outputs.L5:
**Late, For Now**

The train was late, and so was she. He waited beneath the station clock, holding two cups of coffee that had long since gone cold.

At midnight, a message finally appeared on his phone:

*I’m sorry. I can’t come back—not yet.*

He read it twice, then looked down the empty tracks. Some goodbyes were permanent. Others only borrowed the shape of an ending.

He threw away one coffee and kept the other.

It was goodbye, for now.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about discovering bear tracks on a late-winter hike and feeling the presence of someone who is absent.
counterfactuals.output:
The snow had begun to loosen its grip, sinking around the alder roots, shining with a thin blue water beneath the crust. Then, beside the creek, I found the tracks: five dark commas pressed into the thaw, each print wide as an open hand.

The bear had crossed before me, heavy with sleep, carrying the buried year into morning. I knelt and touched the rim where meltwater gathered. The shape was already leaving itself.

All winter I had tried not to look for you. Yet there you were—in the hush between drips, in the cedar’s lifted branches, in the warmth imagined beneath black fur. The woods kept making room for your absence, and filling it: raven-call, windfall, the small gold flame of willow buds.

I followed until the tracks turned uphill and vanished among stones. For a while, my own steps continued beside them. For a while, I could believe the earth remembered every weight it had carried.

Then snow slid from a bough with a soft collapse, and I was alone again—though not as before.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person nature poem set along Rattlesnake Creek, blending grief, faith, humor, and awe. Include a conversation about what to do if a bear appears.
counterfactuals.output:
**Rattlesnake Creek**

I follow Rattlesnake Creek at dawn,  
where water shoulders through granite  
like a hymn that has forgotten the words  
but remembers exactly how to rise.

My grief comes with me—  
an old dog off its leash,  
sniffing every shadow,  
refusing to be called home.

The cottonwoods tremble gold overhead.  
A kingfisher scolds the morning.  
Even the stones shine  
with the unreasonable confidence of saints.

“What if a bear appears?” you ask.

“I’ll stand tall,” I say,  
“speak calmly, and back away.”

“You’ll scream.”

“I’ll speak calmly *while* screaming.”

“And if it charges?”

“I’ll repent very quickly.”

You laugh, and the creek keeps laughing  
long after we stop,  
tumbling over its bright teeth  
as if death were not the end of anything—  
only water changing posture.

I want to believe that.

I want to believe the one I lost  
has entered some wide valley  
where pain drops from the body  
like a wet coat beside the fire.

Then wind moves through the pines,  
deep as an organ note,  
and sunlight strikes the canyon wall  
until every cliff becomes a window.

I stand there, small and astonished,  
my faith no bigger than a pine nut,  
my doubt vast as the mountain’s shadow—  
yet both held gently  
in the same enormous hand.

Downstream, Rattlesnake Creek  
leaps white into the day.

I follow, laughing once,  
weeping once,  
and calling both of them prayer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue in which a hiker places their hands in animal tracks, jokes with a friend about shaved bears, and reflects on how absence can prove presence.
counterfactuals.output:
I kneel where the mud has kept  
what the forest would not say aloud—  
four broad prints, each one brimming  
with rain and the dark grammar of claws.

I place my hands inside them.

Look, I tell you,  
the earth has grown larger hands than mine.

You laugh and ask if I’m certain  
they’re bear tracks.  
Maybe it was a shaved bear, I say,  
trying to pass as an enormous, embarrassed dog.  
We picture it slipping between the pines,  
pink-skinned and indignant,  
searching for its missing coat.

Our laughter startles nothing.  
No branch cracks. No black shape rises.  
Only the wind moves downhill,  
carrying the cold scent of stone.

Still, the bear is here—  
not in fur or breath,  
but in the hollows it has left behind.

Perhaps that is how absence works:  
not emptiness, but pressure remembered;  
a door still swinging,  
a bed holding the shape of sleep,  
mud keeping the weight  
of a vanished body.

I lift my hands. Water fills the prints again.

The bear is gone.

The bear was here.

And for one quiet moment,  
my palms wear the proof.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary prose poem about loss and spiritual disclosure during a mountain hike in early spring, ending with an image comparing thin, roaring air to love.
counterfactuals.output:
At the trailhead, early spring had loosened the earth but not forgiven it. Snow lingered in the shadows of firs, gray as old letters. I climbed with your absence in my pack—weightless, somehow, and heavier than water. Each switchback opened another distance: the town shrinking below, the river becoming a seam of light, my own life reduced to a few roofs and roads I could cover with one hand.

Above the tree line, the wind took everything personally. It entered my sleeves, pressed its cold mouth to my ears. I said your name aloud, not because I expected an answer, but because grief had made a chapel of my body, and even a ruined chapel must ring.

Then the clouds broke. Nothing descended. No voice, no sudden warmth—only granite, thawing moss, a hawk tilting over the ravine. Yet for one clear moment I understood: the holy was not hiding you from me. It was the terrible openness left behind, the space through which all things pass and are changed.

I stood there until my hands went numb, breathing what the mountain could barely spare, while the thin, roaring air moved through me like love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a surreal, emotionally layered piece of nature writing involving bear tracks, skipping stones, sudden grief, dark water, and the uncanny sense that a missing loved one is nearby.
counterfactuals.output:
At the lake’s edge, the bear tracks filled slowly with rain.

They were enormous, each print holding a small, trembling sky. I knelt beside them and placed my hand over one without touching it. The mud smelled of iron and roots. Somewhere across the water, hidden by firs, a branch broke with the clean report of a bone.

You would have said, *Black bear. Not fresh.*

You always knew how long the wild had been gone.

I found seven flat stones beneath the alder roots. The first skipped twice. The second went under at once, as if accepted. The third flickered across the surface so lightly it seemed not to touch the lake at all.

The water was dark—not black, exactly, but the green-black of a door left open at night.

On the fourth stone, grief arrived.

No warning. No memory ushering it in. One moment I was weighing shale in my palm; the next, I was bent over, breathless, while the rain tapped the hood of my coat with a thousand small fingers. Grief had become weather. It had become the bear moving unseen through the trees. It had become the lake, patiently keeping everything that entered it.

Then I heard you laugh.

Not from the trail behind me, nor from the opposite shore, but close—close enough that I turned with the fifth stone raised in my hand.

Nothing stood there.

Only the tracks. Only sword ferns bowed under rain. Only a pale moth opening and closing on the trunk of a cedar, like a mouth trying to remember a name.

Still, the air had changed. It held the warmth of a body recently risen from a chair. I could almost smell the cedar soap you used, the cold wool of your sleeves. For one impossible instant, I knew you were beside me, looking out over the water.

*Throw it lower,* you said, or the rain said. *Use your wrist.*

The fifth stone skipped five times.

The sixth skipped once and then returned, sliding backward over the surface against wind and sense. It came to rest at my feet, dry as a tooth.

I did not throw the seventh.

I put it in the deepest bear track, where it sank halfway into the reflected sky. Around it, the print looked less like evidence of an animal than the mark of some vast hand that had pressed down gently, testing whether the earth was still there.

By then the far shore had vanished into rain. The lake and the clouds had become one dark water, and the trees seemed to grow downward as well as up. I could no longer tell which world I stood in.

Behind me, something breathed.

I waited without turning.

After a while, the breathing matched mine. Then mine matched it. And though I knew the woods were full of creatures, though I knew absence could wear any mask it pleased, I felt your shoulder near my shoulder—almost touching, not quite.

Together, we watched the last rings from the stones widen across the lake.

They traveled farther than they should have.

They did not disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
